prompt: Which statement best describes what 'append is O(1) **amortised**' means? Assume the array starts empty.

options.text: Each append is O(1) on average, assuming the list sizes are random
options.explanation: This describes average-case analysis, which needs a probability distribution. Amortised analysis uses no probability.

options.text: Every individual append takes O(1) time
options.explanation: Not true: the append that triggers a resize copies every element, which is Θ(n), proportional to the n elements already stored. Amortised bounds allow occasional expensive operations. Here n is the append count.

options.text: Append is O(1) except in the worst case, where it is O(n)
options.explanation: This mixes up single-operation worst case with sequence cost. The amortised bound *is* a worst-case bound, over sequences.

options.text: Any sequence of n appends takes O(n) total time, so the cost per append averages to O(1) over the sequence
options.explanation: Correct. Amortised cost is a guarantee about the total for any sequence, even a worst-case one, divided by the number of operations.

workedExample: A resize-triggering append can be expensive. Starting empty, proportionally increasing spare capacity forces many cheap appends between large copies. Their total copying and writing is linear in append count n. Sharing that total across the sequence gives a constant amortised cost without making assumptions about random inputs.

prompt: A doubling array has just filled its available capacity. A colleague charges a full-array copy to every later append. Why is that bound unnecessarily loose for a long sequence starting empty?

options.text: A resize never copies existing items
options.explanation: The copy-on-resize model explicitly copies them.

options.text: Each resize creates many spare slots for later cheap appends
options.explanation: Correct. The copies are spaced geometrically rather than occurring after every append.

options.text: Copying memory costs one operation regardless of length
options.explanation: The model charges one unit per copied element.

options.text: Only random append sequences get expensive resizes
options.explanation: The resize positions follow capacity, not a probability distribution.

workedExample: Follow capacity after a resize. Many later writes fit without another copy. The copied capacities grow geometrically, so their total stays linear in append count. A costly single operation does not justify charging that worst case to every operation in the sequence.

prompt: Why do n single-item append calls to an initially empty CPython list have linear total work under the usual constant-cost reference model?

options.text: Because the list over-allocates by a constant factor, so the copying costs form a geometric series that sums to O(n)
options.explanation: Correct. Proportional spare capacity spaces copying events apart, giving linear total copying. Exact allocation sizes are implementation details.

options.text: Because Python lists are linked lists, so appending never copies
options.explanation: CPython lists are arrays of pointers, not linked lists. They do copy (or reallocate) when they run out of room.

options.text: Because the operating system copies memory in O(1)
options.explanation: Copying k pointers takes time proportional to k. It is fast in practice, but not constant.

options.text: Because Python preallocates enough room for the whole loop
options.explanation: Python can't know how many appends are coming. It grows capacity as needed, in proportion to the current size.

workedExample: Proportional growth means each larger copy also buys proportionally more spare slots. Copy sizes form a geometric progression and the total is linear in append count n. Exact capacities are CPython implementation details; neither linked-list representation nor constant-time memory copying explains the result.
